terms.applies_to: any identifier, docstring, comment, test name, or route segment
terms.why: The long form buys no clarity over the word everyone already says, and it drifts: one file spells it out while its neighbour abbreviates, so neither name is searchable.

terms.use_instead: State the real contract. A function that swallows failures and reports the outcome is `try_<verb>` (for example `try_send_email`), documented as returning whether it succeeded.
terms.why: "Best effort" names an intention rather than a behavior, so the caller cannot tell whether failure raises, returns, or is silent.

terms.applies_to: a database, schema, cache, or record being up to date — identifiers, docstrings, comments, and test names. Money keeps the word.
terms.use_instead: Say which side you mean. Something lacking what it should have is "behind": `database_is_behind`, `services_behind_this_code`, `ServicesBehindReport`. Something that has it is "current": `current_revision`, `is_current`.
terms.why: A currency is money. Reusing it for freshness makes a payment field and a staleness check read as the same subject, so a reader has to reach the surrounding code before knowing which one a name means.

rejected_replacements.why: "current" is the adjective the misuse was built from, not a form of the banned noun. It is the right word for the revision a database is actually at, and `get_current_revision` is the migration runner's own vocabulary.

terms.use_instead: Say which of the three things it does: a guard that raises is `assert_<condition>`, a create-if-missing is `upsert_<noun>` or `create_<noun>`, a start-if-stopped is `start_<thing>`.
terms.why: One word reads the same for all three, so the caller cannot tell whether it returns a value, raises, or has a side effect.

terms.applies_to: a model or object that carries a field
terms.use_instead: Name it for the thing it models, such as `ApiCredential`, `StateRecord`, or `AliasSet`.
terms.why: Every object holds something, so the word distinguishes nothing.

terms.use_instead: `claim`, `claimed_job`, or `ClaimedJob`. Reserve "lock" for lock ownership and expiry.
terms.why: "Lease" blurs the handoff with the lock that protects it.

terms.applies_to: a guard that raises when a condition does not hold — identifiers, docstrings, comments, test names
terms.use_instead: "assert" — `assert_<condition>`, naming the invariant the call site depends on: `assert_membership`, `assert_owner`, `assert_member_has_role`, `assert_access_level`.
terms.why: A guard and the thing it guards read the same when both say "require", so a call site states a wish rather than a condition. "assert" says the check happens here and refusal stops the caller.

rejected_replacements.replacement: Renaming an error code's "_REQUIRED" suffix to "_ASSERTED"
rejected_replacements.why: There the word is an adjective for an unmet precondition, not a guard. Name the state instead: `NOT_A_MEMBER`, `ORGANIZATION_CONTEXT_MISSING`.

terms.use_instead: Name the helper for what it builds: a `<noun>_*_factory` fixture, `create_*`, or "sample data".
terms.why: Setup data is not a seed, and the word hides whether the helper builds, persists, or both.

terms.applies_to: a status or record that has stopped changing
terms.why: Money genuinely settles, so keep the word for payment settlement and nowhere else.

rejected_replacements.why: State-machine jargon a reader has to translate.

terms.applies_to: a subject's current state in some process
terms.use_instead: Name the thing the model actually carries. A model holding a count and a timestamp is `*Attempts`; one holding an outcome is `*Status` or `*Result`.
terms.why: "Standing" reads as a rank or reputation, which is never what these carry.

terms.applies_to: a permission, authorization, or access guard — never input validation
terms.use_instead: `assert_<condition>` for anything gating access: `assert_admin`, `assert_organization_admin`, `assert_revocable_key`. The call site then reads as the condition that must hold, and the weight of the word matches what refusal costs the caller.
terms.why: Checking who may do something is not the same act as checking whether a value is well formed, and one word for both makes a permission gate read like a format check. "validate" stays correct for input: a pydantic validator, a bounds check on a request field, a payload parsed into a model.
rejected_replacements: Banning "validate" outright. It is the right word for input validation, and renaming every field and model validator to assert_ made guards of things that only clean a value.
